title: The hypertrophy series: bypassing muscular endurance thresholds
summary: NH argues that very high-rep sets (15-30) end through artificial failure, a pump or lactic acid safeguard, before the muscle's baseline is truly damaged. He recommends staying mostly in 2-12 reps with only a few exercises around 15, since fiber damage, not metabolic fatigue or pump, drives hypertrophy.
claims: In sets of 15, 20 or 30 reps what stops you is not muscular failure but a safeguard he calls mechanical or artificial failure
Curling an empty bar until the pump forces you to stop does not reach an intensity that damages the baseline
Intensity equivalences break down at high reps: in 3-5 reps the muscle fails, in 15-20 reps the body fails due to lactic acid signals while the muscle is not yet tired
Stay between 2 and 12 reps and keep only a select few exercises around 15 reps; a split mostly in 10-15 reps keeps hitting artificial failure
Heavy squats or bench for 3-5 reps rarely give a pump, and a band press pumps the chest more than a barbell, yet the heavy barbell work builds more muscle
Metabolic fatigue exists but is not the main driver of hypertrophy; fiber damage is
Confusing artificial failure with organic failure leaves gains on the table; pumping the muscle full of lactic acid will not make it grow
exercises: more pump, less growth than barbell bench
